In summary, our research is concerned with

two important issues in the economics of education: the effect of the imperfect labor markets on investments in education and the effect of taxes and subsidies to education on investments in human capital.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the optimal policy is to subsidize education, but not to subsidize physical capital.
the equilibrium is characterized by too little investments in human and too much investments in physical capital.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the equilibrium is characterized by too many workers who invest in education.
, when the distribution of the workers across the sectors is not too skewed toward the low-skill sector, the government should provide subsidies to education.
the optimal tax-subsidy policy consists of a subsidy to education that is financed by a tax on physical capital.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the presence of imperfect labor markets, the effects of subsidies to education on the economy's total expected surplus can be negative.
, when the two sectors are imperfect substitutes, a subsidy to education is not always a Pareto-improvement, and may be welfare-reducing.
the welfare properties of the equilibrium are very sensitive to the distribution of the workers' productivity in the two sectors.
